title: Pseudohyperkalaemia and Glucose-Corrected Sodium
summary: Learn why a high potassium can come from the tube rather than the patient, how to prove it, why the ECG cannot decide, and how to correct a low sodium for hyperglycaemia using the 1.6 and 2.4 factors.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 15 Hit 8 (pseudohyperkalemia), Hit 10 (glucose–sodium correction), Trap 3 (low Na with high glucose) and Trap 4 (haemolysed or fist-clenched K). Checked against Asirvatham 2013, Fujimaru 2025, Umińska 2026, Varga 2019, Baldrighi 2018, Lee 2022 (Korean Society of Nephrology), Chuang 2020 and Mody 2026. The reviewer’s single “1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL” factor is one of two in use (Hillier 2.4 is used by European and Korean guidance; register flag rv-glucose-na-factor). The reviewer’s “no physiologic consequence” is qualified because the same artifacts can mask true hypokalaemia (rv-pseudok-masks-hypok). The reviewer’s checklist lists cold agglutinins (found only as a single case abstract, Mody 2026) but omits cold storage temperature, which the reviews describe (rv-pseudok-cold-storage). The reviewer attributes the normal-ECG point to KDIGO; the KDIGO conference report was not openly available here, so the lesson cites Varga 2019 instead. The reviewer’s own “HIT-FLED” mnemonic is not reproduced. Not taught: pseudohyponatraemia mechanics (taught in chem-pseudohyponatremia-jaffe), hyperkalaemia treatment.

objectives: Explain why small potassium leaks from cells produce large rises in measured potassium.
List collection, contamination and in-tube causes of pseudohyperkalaemia and how to confirm it.
Explain why a normal ECG cannot distinguish true from false hyperkalaemia.
Correct serum sodium for hyperglycaemia and state why the factor is uncertain.

scenes.title: Two suspicious electrolytes
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two results reach the chemistry bench on the same winter morning. (1) An outpatient serum potassium of 6.4 mmol/L; the phlebotomy note says the patient pumped a fist under the tourniquet, the platelet count is 900 × 10⁹/L, and the tube travelled by courier for hours in a cold van. (2) An emergency-department patient with serum sodium 128 mmol/L and glucose 700 mg/dL. Question token: “Real, artifact, or expected?”

cues.text: Two results reach the bench on a cold morning. An outpatient potassium of 6.4: the patient pumped a fist, the platelet count is very high, and the tube sat in a cold courier van.
And an emergency patient with sodium 128 and glucose 700 milligrams per decilitre.
Is each result real, a tube artifact, or an expected consequence of something else?

props.title: 1 Outpatient K⁺ 6.4 mmol/L
lines: Hours in a cold courier van

scenes.title: Why these two numbers mislead
scenes.altText: Schematic. Left card, potassium: about 98% of body potassium is inside cells; the intracellular-to-extracellular ratio is roughly 40:1, so a small leak from cells raises the measured value a lot. Platelets release potassium during clotting, so serum potassium normally runs about 0.36 mmol/L higher than plasma. Right card, sodium: glucose stays outside cells, pulls water out of them and dilutes sodium. Sodium falls while osmolality rises: hypertonic hyponatraemia, a real dilution rather than a measurement error.

cues.text: Potassium first. About ninety-eight percent of the body’s potassium sits inside cells, roughly forty times the concentration outside. A tiny leak from cells shows up as a big rise in the tube.
Even normal clotting releases potassium from platelets, so serum potassium runs about a third of a millimole per litre higher than plasma.
Sodium is different. Glucose stays outside cells, so a high glucose pulls water out of the cells and dilutes the sodium.
The sodium falls while the osmolality rises. This is hypertonic hyponatraemia: a real dilution, not an analytical error.

scenes.title: Where false potassium comes from
scenes.altText: Three cause cards. At the draw: fist clenching (in one study the pumping hand read 1.04 mmol/L higher than the other hand; another review cites rises of up to 1.4 mEq/L with handgrip exercise under a tourniquet), a tourniquet left on for more than 1 minute, and haemolysis from traumatic draws, small needles or forceful syringe transfer. Contamination: potassium EDTA carried over when the order of draw is broken, or potassium-containing IV fluid; heavy EDTA contamination also lowers calcium, magnesium, zinc and ALP. In the tube: thrombocytosis and leukocytosis release potassium during clotting; delayed processing exhausts glucose so the sodium–potassium pump fails; cold storage inhibits the pump (seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia); familial pseudohyperkalaemia is a rare inherited red-cell leak; in cold agglutinin disease, cooling the sample can agglutinate and lyse red cells in vitro (reported in a case abstract).

cues.text: At the draw: fist clenching releases potassium from forearm muscle. In one study the pumping hand read about one millimole per litre higher than the other. A tourniquet left on for over a minute, or a traumatic draw that haemolyses the sample, adds more.
Contamination: potassium EDTA carried over when the order of draw is broken, or a drip containing potassium. Heavy EDTA contamination also drags calcium and magnesium down, a useful clue.
In the tube: very high platelet or white cell counts release potassium as the sample clots. Delay uses up glucose, the sodium potassium pump stops, and potassium leaks out.

Cold storage also stops the pump, so winter courier samples can show seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia. A rare inherited red cell leak behaves the same way, and one case report describes cold agglutinins lysing red cells in a cooled tube.

lines: Delay: pump runs out of fuel

scenes.title: Proving it, and correcting sodium
scenes.altText: Workup card: suspect pseudohyperkalaemia when potassium is discordant with prior results or the clinical picture; consult the laboratory and recollect without fist clenching or a prolonged tourniquet. With thrombocytosis or leukocytosis, collect heparin plasma and analyse promptly; some authors define pseudohyperkalaemia as a serum-minus-plasma difference above 0.4 mmol/L. Caution: in leukaemia or lymphoma (one report in CLL), heparin plasma can itself be falsely high (reverse pseudohyperkalaemia). ECG card: in one emergency-department study, more than half of hyperkalaemic patients had no ECG change suggestive of hyperkalaemia, and 24% of normokalaemic patients did, so the ECG cannot settle it. Sodium card: corrected Na⁺ = measured Na⁺ + factor × (glucose − 100)/100; Katz 1.6 (cited by ADA hyperglycaemic-crisis guidance), Hillier 2.4 (used in European and Korean hyponatraemia guidance); Hillier noted underestimation above 400 mg/dL, where about 4 fits better. Hook answers: (1) potassium: recollect correctly, heparin plasma, prompt analysis; (2) sodium: 128 + 1.6 × 6 ≈ 138 or 128 + 2.4 × 6 ≈ 142, both within 135–145, though above 400 mg/dL Hillier found even 2.4 too small, so the true value may be higher still.

cues.text: Suspect an artifact when the potassium clashes with earlier results or the clinical picture. Call the lab and recollect: no fist clenching, a short tourniquet. With high platelet or white cell counts, use heparin plasma analysed promptly. Some authors define pseudohyperkalaemia as serum more than 0.4 above plasma.

Two cautions. In leukaemia or lymphoma, heparin plasma can itself read falsely high. And the ECG cannot settle it: in one study more than half of truly hyperkalaemic patients had no suggestive ECG change.

Now sodium. Corrected sodium equals measured sodium plus a factor for each 100 milligrams per decilitre of glucose above 100. The classic factor is 1.6; European and Korean hyponatraemia guidance uses 2.4, and above 400 the shift is larger still.

Back to the hook. The potassium needs a careful redraw into heparin plasma, run promptly. The sodium corrects to about 138 with 1.6, or 142 with 2.4, perhaps more at a glucose this high. The low reading is explained by glucose.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A haemolysed or fist-clenched high K⁺ means hyperkalaemia” (✓ suspect the tube and recollect; the same artifacts can also push a truly low potassium into the reference interval); “A normal ECG proves pseudohyperkalaemia” (✓ many truly hyperkalaemic patients have no suggestive ECG change); “Low Na⁺ with very high glucose is ordinary hypotonic hyponatraemia” (✓ water shift; osmolality is high; correct the sodium first).

cues.text: Trap one: a haemolysed or fist-clenched high potassium means hyperkalaemia. No: suspect the tube and recollect. The same artifacts can even hide a truly low potassium.
Trap two: a normal ECG proves the potassium is false. No: many patients with true hyperkalaemia have a normal-looking ECG.
Trap three: low sodium with very high glucose is ordinary hypotonic hyponatraemia. No: glucose pulled water out of cells, osmolality is high, and the sodium must be corrected first.

scenes.title: Squeeze, spill, sit, chill
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Squeeze, spill, sit, chill: four ways the TUBE gets potassium the patient never had — SQUEEZE (fist, tourniquet, rough draw), SPILL (EDTA or IV fluid), SIT (delay, clotting platelets and white cells), CHILL (cold storage, cold agglutinins). And for sodium: sugar borrows water — add 1.6 to 2.4 per 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: squeeze, spill, sit, chill. Squeeze the arm or fist, spill EDTA or a drip, let the tube sit, or chill it, and the tube gains potassium the patient never had. For sodium: sugar borrows water, so add 1.6 to 2.4 for every 100 of glucose above 100.

Where it breaks: the list is not complete, since inherited red cell leaks and heparin effects in leukaemia exist too; the same artifacts can hide a low potassium; and the sodium factor is an approximation with no single agreed value, too small at very high glucose.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “High K⁺: squeeze, spill, sit, chill → recollect, heparin plasma; ECG cannot decide”, “High glucose: corrected Na⁺ = Na⁺ + 1.6–2.4 × (glucose − 100)/100”.

cues.text: Treat an unexpected high potassium as a possible tube artifact and recollect carefully, since a normal ECG cannot decide, and correct a low sodium for high glucose by about 1.6 to 2.4 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL before classifying the hyponatraemia.

props.label: High K⁺: squeeze · spill · sit · chill → recollect; ECG can’t decide

explanation.what: Plain language: a potassium result can be high because potassium leaked out of cells in the tube, not because the patient has too much; and a sodium can look low because high glucose pulled water into the blood and diluted it. Scientific terms: pseudohyperkalaemia (spurious or factitious hyperkalaemia), haemolysis index, K₂EDTA contamination, order of draw, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, reverse pseudohyperkalaemia, familial pseudohyperkalaemia, seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia, masked hypokalaemia, hypertonic (translocational) hyponatraemia, corrected sodium.
explanation.why: About 98% of body potassium is intracellular, so a small leak changes the measured extracellular value a lot. Glucose is largely confined to the extracellular space, so hyperglycaemia draws water out of cells and lowers sodium while raising osmolality.
explanation.measure: Pseudohyperkalaemia: recollect without fist clenching or prolonged tourniquet; with thrombocytosis or leukocytosis use heparin plasma analysed promptly; a serum–plasma difference > 0.4 mmol/L has been used as a definition; serum normally exceeds plasma by about 0.36 mmol/L. Corrected Na⁺ = measured Na⁺ + factor × (glucose − 100)/100, factor 1.6 (Katz) or 2.4 (Hillier); above 400 mg/dL about 4 fits better.
explanation.differs: Pseudohyperkalaemia (tube) vs true hyperkalaemia (patient); serum vs heparin plasma; reverse pseudohyperkalaemia (heparin plasma falsely high in leukaemia); hypertonic hyponatraemia from glucose vs hypotonic hyponatraemia; Katz 1.6 vs Hillier 2.4.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the best next step for a high potassium with fist clenching, haemolysis or thrombocytosis (recollect, heparin plasma); recognising that a normal ECG does not prove the result is false; and calculating corrected sodium in hyperglycaemia.

mnemonic.text: Squeeze, spill, sit, chill: four ways the tube gains potassium the patient never had (squeeze = fist, tourniquet, rough draw; spill = EDTA or IV fluid; sit = delay, clotting platelets and white cells; chill = cold storage or cold agglutinins). For sodium: sugar borrows water, so add 1.6 to 2.4 per 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100.
mnemonic.explanation: Groups pseudohyperkalaemia causes by where they happen and pairs them with the sodium correction.
mnemonic.limitation: Not exhaustive (familial red-cell leak, heparin effect in leukaemia, alcohol antiseptic); the same artifacts can hide a truly low potassium; the sodium factor is an approximation with no consensus value and underestimates the fall above about 400 mg/dL.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic outpatient has serum potassium 6.3 mmol/L. The patient clenched a fist repeatedly during the draw and the platelet count is 950 × 10⁹/L. What is the best next step?

options.text: Recollect without fist clenching into a heparin tube and analyse promptly
options.rationale: Correct. Fist clenching and thrombocytosis both release potassium in vitro; heparin plasma avoids release from clotting platelets.

options.text: Accept it as pseudohyperkalaemia because the ECG is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal ECG cannot confirm pseudohyperkalaemia: in one emergency-department study more than half of truly hyperkalaemic patients had no suggestive ECG change.

options.text: Correct the potassium using the platelet count and report
options.rationale: Incorrect. A corrected potassium may be unreliable because several interacting factors may not be measurable; a proper recollection answers the question.

options.text: Recollect into a K₂EDTA tube to avoid clotting
options.rationale: Incorrect. K₂EDTA contains potassium and itself falsely raises the result.

questions.stem: A patient has measured sodium 126 mmol/L and glucose 600 mg/dL. Using the Katz factor of 1.6 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL above 100 mg/dL, what is the corrected sodium?

options.rationale: Incorrect. This uses the Hillier factor (126 + 2.4 × 5 = 138), not the Katz factor asked for.
Incorrect. This multiplies 1.6 by 6, forgetting to subtract the normal 100 mg/dL first.
Incorrect. The correction is added, because glucose lowered the measured sodium.

questions.stem: Which statement about hyperglycaemia and serum sodium is correct?

options.text: Glucose draws water out of cells, so sodium falls while measured osmolality is raised
options.rationale: Correct. This is hypertonic hyponatraemia caused by a real water shift.

options.text: It is an analytical error; the sodium in the patient is actually normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Glucose causes a real water shift out of cells that dilutes the sodium in the patient; it is not a measurement error.
Incorrect. Glucose is an effective osmole, so osmolality is normal or high.

options.text: All guidelines agree on a 1.6 mmol/L correction factor
options.rationale: Incorrect. Factors of 1.6 (Katz) and 2.4 (Hillier) are both used, with no consensus.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 15 Hit 10 and Trap 3 give a single factor of 1.6 mEq/L per 100 mg/dL glucose. Baldrighi 2018 reports no consensus between Katz 1.6 and Hillier 2.4 (Hillier also found underestimation above 400 mg/dL, where about 4 fits better); the Korean Society of Nephrology 2022 recommendations and the European guideline (as reported by Baldrighi) use 2.4. The lesson teaches both factors (register flag rv-glucose-na-factor).

Ch. 15 Hit 8 and Trap 4 say pseudohyperkalemia has no physiologic consequence. That is true of the potassium in the patient, but Asirvatham 2013 notes that the same artifacts can push a truly low potassium into the reference interval (masked hypokalaemia), and Fujimaru 2025 notes the risk of unnecessary treatment (register flag rv-pseudok-masks-hypok).

Ch. 15 Hit 8, Trap 4 and the HIT-FLED memory hook list cold agglutinins (supported only at case-report level, Mody 2026) but omit cold storage or transport temperature, which Asirvatham 2013, Fujimaru 2025 and Umińska 2026 describe as a cause through Na/K pump inhibition (seasonal pseudohyperkalaemia). The lesson teaches cold storage and mentions cold agglutinins as a case report (register flag rv-pseudok-cold-storage).
